Pretest
Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Define, diagnose, and stage Preiser disease according to the Herbert-Lanzetta staging system
and the Kalainov criteria.
Define, diagnose, and stage Kienböck disease according to the Lichtman classification system.
Assess nonsurgical and surgical approaches considered for various stages of Preiser disease
and Kienböck disease.
Introduction
Osteonecrosis of the scaphoid—first described by Georg Preiser in 19101—is a rare cause of
wrist pain and stiffness.

Osteonecrosis of the lunate, also described in 1910 by Robert Kienböck, was identified using
the relatively new radiographic technology at that time.2
The causes of Preiser disease and Kienböck disease are unknown (idiopathic). Postulated
factors include trauma, corticosteroid use, skeletal variations, and hypercoagulable conditions.
The pathology and natural history of both conditions are incompletely understood and difficult
to study because they are uncommon.
Treatment options are a subject of debate.
Preiser Disease
Overview
Patients with symptoms related to Preiser disease typically report pain on the radial side of the
wrist.
They may be tender in the anatomic snuffbox.
Similar to most intra-articular processes, some loss of passive wrist motion usually is present.
Branches of the radial artery enter the distal pole of the scaphoid, and the proximal portion is
mostly supplied via retrograde interosseous flow. This has been proposed to render the
proximal pole susceptible to osteonecrosis.3
Radiographs can identify Preiser disease unless it is mild.
MRI may be helpful if the disease is suspected and in early stages with no radiographic
changes.
Loss of marrow fat causes decreased signal on T1-weighted images.
T2-weighted images also reveal low signal intensity.
CT may help characterize bony fragmentation, which can be a nudge toward salvage
procedures.
In 1994, Herbert and Lanzetta4 described a radiographic staging system intended to facilitate
decision making:
Stage I: normal radiographs, positive bone scan
Stage II: increased density of proximal pole and generalized osteoporosis
Stage III: fragmentation of proximal pole
Stage IV: carpal collapse, osteoarthritis
Kalainov et al3 distinguished complete osteonecrosis (type 1) and partial osteonecrosis (type 2,
usually proximal pole involvement) based on MRI appearance.

According to the authors’ observations, type 1 scaphoids are expected to fragment, whereas
type 2 scaphoids retain their structure.

Overview
The relationship between staging, management, and outcome is a subject of debate.
Advanced wrist arthritis seemingly related to Preiser disease is exceedingly rare,
suggesting that stage IV disease may be more theoretical.
Nonsurgical Management
No consensus exists with regard to management because of the rarity of Preiser disease and
questions about the natural history of the condition.
Nonsurgical management is palliative (symptom alleviation) rather than disease-modifying
(altering the natural history of osteonecrosis). It may include splint immobilization, anti-
inflammatory medications, and cortisone injections.
Injections should be used sparingly because of the known association between steroid use
and osteonecrosis, particularly in the hip literature; however, the long-term risks associated
with repeated cortisone injections in the wrist are not well understood.
The role of surgical management is a subject of debate.

Nonsurgical Management
Tomori et al5 described eight patients treated via a mean of 1.8 months of splint
immobilization for stage I through stage III disease according to the Herbert-Lanzetta
classification system. MRI revealed four patients with complete and four patients with
partial involvement of the scaphoid. Radiographic disease progression occurred in five of
the eight patients, and none of the patients experienced relief of symptoms. All eight
patients accepted an offer of surgical treatment.

Claessen et al6 described the 15-year experience at one hospital. Among 18 patients (13
Herbert-Lanzetta stage II, 4 stage III, and 1 stage IV) only 2 patients elected to undergo
surgical treatment.
Surgical Management
Various surgical treatment options have been described for Preiser disease.
Vascularized Bone Graft
If preoperative radiographs demonstrate no signs of radiocarpal arthritis or carpal
malalignment (Herbert-Lanzetta stages I and II), vascularized bone grafting (VBG) is an option.
Relative contraindications include carpal malalignment with or without degenerative changes.
Caution is warranted in patients who have undergone prior surgical procedures, in whom the
potential vascular pedicles may be disrupted.

Vascularized Bone Graft
Technique: The scaphoid is prepared with the use of power burrs and curets to create a
dorsal cortical window. Necrotic bone is débrided, preserving the cortical shell. The 1,2
intercompartmental supraretinacular artery and the 2,3 intercompartmental
supraretinacular artery are pedicled bone grafts that are commonly used. The bone graft
can be rotated to the affected area of the scaphoid and secured via a press-fit technique
or Kirschner wire fixation. If used, Kirschner wires can be removed after 6 to 8 weeks.
Moran et al7 described eight patients treated via VBG and reported pain alleviation and
preserved radiocarpal wrist motion despite incomplete proximal pole revascularization.
Whether these results are better than the natural history of the illness remains unclear.
Radial wedge osteotomy

Closing radial wedge osteotomies may be considered for all four Herbert-Lanzetta stages of
Preiser disease.8
The rationale for a closing radial wedge osteotomy is attenuation of axial pressure on the wrist
joint.
This approach is less invasive than salvage procedures, such as proximal row carpectomy or
wrist arthrodesis, and simpler to perform than VBG.

Radial Wedge Osteotomy
Technique: A standard volar-radial approach to the distal radius is used, and a closing
wedge is performed through the metaphyseal bone. Fixation can be achieved with the
use of a distal radial volar locking plate. Patients are immobilized for 4 to 6 weeks and
then work on regaining wrist motion (Figure 1).
Figure 1 PA radiographs of a wrist with Preiser disease. A, Preoperative radiograph
demonstrates collapse of the scaphoid proximal pole. B, Postoperative radiograph

Preiser’s disease: A case report. J Hand Surg Am 2006;31[7]:1154-1156.)
Scaphoid excision with intercarpal fusion
Scaphoid excision with limited wrist fusion is an option for patients with degenerative changes.
In patients without evidence of carpal malalignment or notable arthritis, other surgical
procedures can take priority.
Technique: Standard fixation of the intercarpal fusion with the use of Kirschner wires, circular
plates, or staples can be performed. Patients typically are immobilized for 4 to 6 weeks.
Proximal row carpectomy
Similar to scaphoid excision with four-corner intercarpal fusion, proximal row carpectomy
typically is performed in patients with degenerative joint changes and/or in whom the
scaphoid is not salvageable. It is an option if the lunate fossa of the radius is well preserved.
Some surgeons consider this option less suitable for patients younger than 45 years because
of the potential for future arthrosis; however, whether important differences exist compared
with other procedures that maintain wrist motion remains unclear.
Arthrosis of the capitate should be limited; however, some have suggested interposition of a
dorsal capsular flap.
Technique: Excision of the scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum is performed while maintaining
the integrity of the radioscaphocapitate ligament to prevent ulnar translocation of the carpus.
The distal pole of the scaphoid can be left if preferred; however, radial styloidectomy may be
considered to limit postoperative impingement. The wrist may be immobilized for 4 weeks.
Kienböck Disease
Overview
The cause of osteonecrosis of the lunate is unknown (idiopathic).
Speculation exists that vascular anatomy and relative force transfer through the radius may be
related. Gelberman et al9 described three different vessel patterns in the lunate and found
that 31% are supplied by a single intraosseous arterial path with minimal arborization.

Lichtman et al10 proposed a staging classification for Kienböck disease based on radiography
(Figure 2; Resource 1).
Stage I: no visible changes on radiographs, changes observed on MRI
Stage II: sclerosis of the lunate
Stage IIIa: fragmentation of the lunate
Stage IIIb: fragmentation of the lunate, fixed rotation/flexion of the scaphoid
Stage IV: degeneration of adjacent intercarpal joints

Figure 2 Drawings (left) and imaging studies (right) of the wrist show the stages of Kienböck
disease according to Lichtman. In stage I, the trabecular bone has not yet been destroyed, and
plain radiographs are normal or demonstrate a linear fracture without sclerosis or collapse of the
lunate. In stage II, radiographs demonstrate increased density of the lunate, frequently with one
or more fracture lines; the entire lunate may be sclerotic, but lunate height is preserved. In stage
IIIA, radiographs demonstrate lunate collapse; however, carpal height is relatively unchanged. In
stage IIIB, radiographs demonstrate proximal migration of the capitate and fixed hyperflexion of

the scaphoid (cortical ring sign). In stage IV, arthritic changes are observed throughout the
radiocarpal and/or midcarpal joint. The reformatted coronal CT scan shows radial styloid and
radiolunate degenerative changes. (Reproduced from Allan CH, Joshi A, Lichtman DM: Kienböck’s
disease: Diagnosis and treatment. J Am Acad Orthop Surg 2001;9[2]:128-136.)
In 2006, Bain and Begg11 described a classification system based on arthroscopic findings and
the premise that radiographic evaluation may underestimate articular changes and that
arthroscopic findings may alter treatment recommendations for patients with Kienböck
disease.
Grade 0: all articular surfaces normal
Grade 1: abnormal proximal lunate articular surface
Grade 2a: two abnormal surfaces
Proximal lunate and lunate facet abnormal
Grade 2b: two abnormal surfaces
Proximal and distal lunate abnormal
Grade 3: three abnormal surfaces
Capitate surface usually preserved
Grade 4: all four articular surfaces abnormal

Overview
Kienböck disease usually is diagnosed in the dominant wrists of men aged 15 to 40
years. Radiographs show all but the mildest disease. MRI also may help differentiate
Kienböck disease from other causes of wrist pain, such as ulnar impaction syndrome
(Figure 3).

Figure 3 Coronal T1-weighted MRIs of a wrist with Kienböck disease (A) and a wrist with
ulnar impaction syndrome (B). Note the involvement of the entire lunate in the wrist with
Kienböck disease. (Courtesy of Eon K. Shin, MD, Philadelphia, PA.)
The Lichtman classification often is used to guide treatment decisions. A consensus
regarding the treatment approach for Kienböck disease is difficult to attain because the
etiology is unknown and the natural history is poorly understood. Other factors may be
considered in the decision-making process.
Given the theory that Kienböck disease may be related to relative axial wrist force
transfer through the radius, patients with Kienböck disease and ulnar negative variance
commonly are offered an osteotomy to shorten the radius, based on the rationale that
this will decrease loads on the lunate. The degree to which an osteotomy relieves
symptoms through specific rather than nonspecific mechanisms is unknown because no
simulated surgical controlled trials have been performed. The ability of an osteotomy to
alter the natural history of the disease also is unknown.
Rhee et al12 associated a medial hamate facet (type 2 lunate) with a lower risk of coronal
plane fracture and scaphoid flexion deformity, suggesting this may inhibit the

progression of Kienböck disease. Therefore, lunate morphology may be considered in
selecting a treatment course.
Treatment Approaches
Numerous surgical procedures have been described for the management of Kienböck disease.
Lichtman staging often serves as a guide for management; however, other factors may be
considered.
Stage I
A period of immobilization is an option for patients with symptoms ascribed to Kienböck
disease. Immobilization for as long as 4 months is described.
Given that a trial of immobilization trial has not proved to alter disease progression and that
the prospect of prolonged immobilization is associated with a considerable financial and
mental burden, this option may be declined.
Stage II and Stage IIIa
With ulnar negative variance, a radial shortening osteotomy or ulnar lengthening are
considered based on the rationale that they will reduce load on the lunate (Figure 4).
Radial shortening osteotomies are preferred because of concerns regarding potential
nonunion with ulnar lengthening.

wrist in which a radial shortening osteotomy was performed to manage stage II Kienböck disease.

If the ulnar variance is neutral or positive, the load experienced by the lunate can be reduced
by performing a capitate shortening osteotomy.
This is performed by making an oblique saw cut through the mid-body of the capitate and
securing the osteotomy site with the use of headless compression screws (Figure 5).
Whether these procedures alter the natural history of Kienböck disease and whether they
are more palliative than a simulated procedure (ie, better than placebo;) a necessary test to
be confident about subjective outcomes) remains unclear.

Figure 5 Preoperative PA and lateral (A) radiographs and postoperative PA and lateral (B)
fluoroscopic images of a wrist in which a capitate shortening osteotomy was performed to
manage stage IIIa Kienböck disease. Note the oblique osteotomy through the capitate and the
angled insertion of the headless compression screws. (Courtesy of Eon K. Shin, MD, Philadelphia,
PA.)
VBG is an option for Kienböck stage II and stage III disease.
VBG is not proven to be disease-modifying. In many patients, additional deterioration occurs.
VBG is reported to alleviate pain but has not been compared with controls, specifically
simulated surgery controls.
In a VBG procedure, necrotic portions of the lunate are débrided with the use of burrs and
curets, and a pedicled VBG is rotated to the lunate and secured via press-fit or Kirschner
wires (Figure 6).
Various pedicled grafts have been described, including those from the metacarpal base and
the distal radius.16
Free vascularized flaps also have been used, including the medial femoral condyle, medial
femoral trochlea, and iliac crest.

Figure 6 Preoperative (A) and postoperative (B) PA radiographs of a wrist with stage II Kienböck
disease. A vascularized bone graft from the distal radius was impacted into the débrided lunate
via a dorsal cortical window. A spanning plate was applied to decrease contact pressures across
the lunate. (Courtesy of Eon K. Shin, MD, Philadelphia, PA.)
Distal radius and ulnar metaphyseal core decompression has been described as a possible
treatment option for Kienböck disease.17
In the procedure as first described, a cortical window is created in the distal radius and ulna.
The cancellous bone is curetted and impacted but not removed.
The rationale for core decompression was developed after noting spontaneous resolution of
Kienböck disease after a nondisplaced distal radius fracture. The resolution was attributed to
increased vascularity during healing. Core decompression may alter the vascular milieu
rather than specifically altering the biomechanics of the carpus.

Studies suggest outcomes similar to other treatment options. None of these procedures may
alter the natural history of the disease or palliate better than simulated surgery, making
them all comparable.
Stage IIIb
Symptomatic patients with fixed rotation or flexion deformities of the scaphoid may be
offered a salvage reconstructive procedure, such as proximal row carpectomy,
scaphotrapeziotrapezoid (STT) arthrodesis, or scaphocapitate arthrodesis with lunate
excision (Figure 7).
A scaphotrapeziotrapezoid arthrodesis may reduce load on the lunate by correcting the
flexed scaphoid position.
Limited wrist fusions also represent a motion-sparing salvage option in patients with
chondral loss at the capitate head, which would preclude a proximal row carpectomy.
Although ulnar translocation has been described as a potential complication after
scaphocapitate arthrodesis, studies have suggested that additional surgery rarely is needed
to address this problem.
Figure 7 Preoperative PA and lateral (A) and postoperative PA and lateral (B) radiographs of a
wrist with stage IIIa/stage IIIb Kienböck disease. Given the degree of lunate fragmentation and

Stage IV
Proximal row carpectomy, total wrist arthrodesis, or total wrist arthroplasty are salvage
options for patients with symptomatic disease associated with degenerative changes.
Salvage procedures also may be an option for patients who are not satisfied with their
symptoms after recovering from a prior surgical procedure (Figure 8).
If the cartilage in the proximal pole of the capitate or lunate fossa of the radius is poor,
proximal row carpectomy can be combined with dorsal capsule interposition; capitate
resurfacing with the use of a pyrocarbon implant also has been described.22


Treatment Approaches
Delaere et al13 retrospectively compared surgical and nonsurgical treatment strategies
and found that surgical management resulted in a 24% loss of wrist motion and a
considerable need to change work and leisure activities. The authors concluded that
surgical management did not demonstrate clear superiority over nonsurgical
management for early Kienböck disease.
van Leeuwen et al14 compared radiographic progression of Kienböck disease in 48
patients after a radial shortening osteotomy or nonsurgical treatment and found very
small loss of carpal height over a minimum of 1 year, no change in more than one-half of
patients, and no difference between surgical and nonsurgical management.
Salmon et al15 compared 18 nonsurgically treated patients with 15 patents who
underwent a radial shortening osteotomy at a mean of 3.6 years after diagnosis (range,
1.5 to 9 years). All patients had stage II or stage III disease. Patients treated surgically
reported less pain but had comparable mean motion (73% versus 62%), mean grip
strength (75% versus 61%), carpal height (0.7 for both), and increase in lunate width (2.4
mm versus 2.0 mm) compared with the patients treated nonsurgically.
Koh et al18 reported long-term improvement in patient satisfaction and wrist range of
motion after radial shortening; however, 73% of patients had radiographic evidence of
wrist deterioration at a minimum follow-up of 10 years. Moran et al16 retrospectively
reviewed patients with mid- to late-stage disease using the dorsal 4 + 5 extensor
compartment artery pedicled bone graft. At a mean follow-up of 31 months, the authors
documented improved range of motion, grip strength, and Mayo wrist scores, with 92%
reporting pain improvement. Patients who had an MRI signal consistent with improved
vascularity had higher Mayo wrist scores and were more likely to return to work.
Illarramendi et al17 found that 16 of 22 patients (most with stage II or stage IIIa disease)
who underwent core decompression reported less pain, with no reported complications

at a mean follow-up of 10 years. Follow-up radiographs revealed the same preoperative
Lichtman stage in 17 of the 22 patients.
Among 18 wrists evaluated by Charre et al19 at a mean of 11 years after scaphocapitate
arthrodesis with concomitant lunate excision for advanced Kienböck disease, pain
alleviation and satisfactory grip strength were maintained. One nonunion was noted.
Similarly, favorable findings also were reported by Luegmair and Saffar20 and Rhee et
al.21
Pearls
Preiser disease and Kienböck disease are idiopathic. Vascular and mechanical theories
predominate but are not established experimentally.
The natural history is unknown, and no proven disease-modifying interventions exist.
Surgical treatment has not proved to be palliative beyond nonspecific effects, making
nonsurgical treatment an option for all patients.
Given the relative rarity of carpal bone osteonecrosis, an unclear natural history, and difficulty
proving palliation to be better than nonspecific effects, a consensus on best practices may be
difficult to reach.
Surgeons should correct common misconceptions (eg, “it hurts, so something must be done,”
“doing something must be better than letting the problem take its natural course”); the factors
that matter most to each patient can direct treatment.
Summary
Preiser disease and Kienböck disease represent osteonecrosis of the scaphoid and lunate,
respectively. Both conditions progress unpredictably, which complicates decision making.
Wide surgeon-to-surgeon variation exists in diagnostic and therapeutic strategies, and little
evidence is available to guide decision making.
